items.title: Halting Biodiversity Loss Requires a Different Kind of Management Research
items.headline: Corporate actions alone cannot stop biodiversity loss
bullets: Reviewed findings from the first business and biodiversity assessment by IPBES.
Found that voluntary corporate actions cannot stop biodiversity loss without wider system shifts.
Urges management research to shift from individual firms to wider economic and political systems.

plain.question: Can voluntary company actions stop the loss of nature and biodiversity?
plain.method: Examined the first major global business and biodiversity assessment report.
plain.finding: Voluntary company steps are not enough without larger changes in policy, money, and society.
plain.why: Management research must change its focus to broader systems instead of looking only at single firms.

full.explainer: A recent major global assessment by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services concluded that voluntary corporate actions alone cannot stop biodiversity loss. To truly protect nature, there must be broader shifts in the policy, economic, financial, social, and knowledge systems that guide business behavior and environmental results. However, current management research on biodiversity mostly focuses on individual firms—what single companies measure, disclose, and do—while ignoring these larger systemic issues. To fix this, researchers propose four new priorities: studying the political economy of inaction, understanding the limits of organizational capability, testing ways to organize beyond economic growth, and rethinking how firms relate to nature. Pursuing these goals requires work that crosses different academic disciplines and teams up with the real-world actors who shape and experience biodiversity outcomes to co-create useful knowledge.

items.title: Land use transitions drive ecosystem service supply–demand balance: spatiotemporal assessment and risk zoning in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area (Hubei section)
items.headline: Land use shifts drive ecosystem supply and demand
bullets: Used InVEST and multiple regression to study ecosystem services from 2000 to 2020.
Found land use changes are the leading driver, causing soil retention deficits.
Categorized zones into risk areas to support customized land management.

plain.question: How do changes in land use affect the balance of nature's benefits and human needs over time?
plain.method: They used computer models and maps to track land changes, water yield, carbon storage, food, and soil retention.
plain.finding: Land changes caused major shifts in the balance of benefits, with soil retention staying in deficit.
plain.why: It helps divide regions into risk zones to plan better land management and protect nature.

full.explainer: This paper looks at how human activities and land changes alter the balance between what nature provides and what people need. Focusing on an ecologically vulnerable region from 2000 to 2020, the researchers studied four main benefits: water yield, carbon storage, food production, and soil retention. By combining land use maps with computer models like InVEST, they tracked how these benefits changed over time. They discovered that shifts between cropland, forest, and built-up areas were the main drivers of the changes. While carbon storage, food, and water improved, soil retention remained in deficit. Statistical tests showed that land use alone accounted for over half of the variation in these benefits. By grouping areas with similar changes, the researchers mapped out risk zones—such as high-risk and stable areas—to help local leaders plan better land management and protect the environment.
caveats: The study focuses on the Three Gorges Reservoir Area, so results may differ elsewhere.
Soil retention remained in deficit, but exact flood or economic risks are not stated.

items.title: Blue-Green Infrastructure as a Territorial Planning Instrument: Quantifying the Contributions of Land Use Change and Climate Forcing to 2050 Flood Risk in a Peri-Urban Coastal Watershed, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
items.headline: Land changes drive future floods more than climate
bullets: Modeled 2050 flood risk under different land and climate futures
Uncontrolled growth doubled high-risk areas while climate alone grew less
Helps plan better land use and green infrastructure to cut flood risk

plain.question: How will future land changes and climate shifts affect urban flood risks?
plain.method: They used a computer flood model to test different 2050 growth and climate futures.
plain.finding: Bad land growth increased flood depths and risks much more than climate changes alone.
plain.why: It shows that smart land planning can protect cities from future floods.

full.explainer: This study looks at how future flooding in a coastal watershed in Rio de Janeiro will be affected by two things: changes in how land is used, and changes in the climate. The researchers tested twelve different futures for the year 2050. These combined three different urban growth paths—ranging from uncontrolled development to a planned path using nature-based solutions and moving people out of danger zones—with different levels of heavy rain and sea-level rise. They used a computer model to simulate floods and created a risk index based on water depth and exposure. Their results show that uncontrolled urban growth causes much worse flooding across the area than climate change does on its own. Only the planned scenario, which included green infrastructure and relocating residents, successfully reduced overall flood risk and increased safe areas compared to the baseline. This proves that local land management plays a massive role in future flood safety.
caveats: Results are specific to this watershed, scenario set, and 2050 horizon.
The computer model represented open channels but not the storm sewer network.

items.title: Morphological and thermal validation of LCZs: Applicability of the LCZ scheme in heterogeneous arid urban environments
items.headline: Testing Local Climate Zones in an arid city
bullets: Used GIS, field surveys, and temperature sensors to test climate zones in Mendoza.
Found thermal differences between dense zones and vegetated, low-density zones.
Shows international climate zones need local validation in unique arid cities.

plain.question: Do standard climate zones work in dry cities with lots of plants?
plain.method: We used maps, camera photos, field checks, and air temperature sensors.
plain.finding: Dense areas stayed warmer while vegetated areas differed, but standard zones need local updates.
plain.why: Helps planners make dry cities more resilient by using accurate local climate data.

full.explainer: This study tests how well a standard global classification system, called Local Climate Zones, applies to the dry urban environment of Mendoza, Argentina. Many cities have open layouts and lots of linear plants that do not fit standard global models easily. The researchers checked the physical shapes of these zones using geographic tools, camera photos, and field surveys. They also checked air temperatures using sensors during the summer of 2021. The results show that dense zones are very similar in structure and temperature, while low-density and vegetated zones differ clearly. However, the data also reveals that global reference values cannot be copied directly into unique, heterogeneous cities without local checks first. Even though thermal data suggested grouping some zones together, physical differences mean keeping six separate classes is best. This replicable method gives useful insights for sustainable urban planning in similar dry and complex settings.
caveats: Thermal data collected only during the summer of 2021
Focuses specifically on the Metropolitan Area of Mendoza

bullets: Mapped building orientations and green areas in an Antalya neighborhood

plain.question: How are buildings facing in a warm climate zone, and how does that affect climate?
plain.method: They used satellite maps and software to check the angles of buildings, plus field checks for green spaces.
plain.finding: More than half of the buildings are turned the wrong way, and there are not enough green areas.
plain.why: Poor building direction makes heat worse, but better landscape design can help fix it.

full.explainer: This paper looks at how buildings are angled in a neighborhood in Antalya, Turkey, to see if they fit a climate-sensitive approach. With global warming and rising energy use, how buildings face the sun matters a lot in hot places. The researchers used digital maps and computer tools to measure the angles of existing buildings compared to the south. They also checked green space using a vegetation index and field observations. The results show that only a small portion of buildings have an ideal orientation, while more than half are poorly oriented. Green space in the area is also very limited. The study concludes that landscape design can act as a useful tool to reduce the disadvantages caused by bad building layouts. For the future, the authors suggest combining architecture and landscape design so new buildings can block unwanted summer sun and make better use of winter sun.
caveats: Study is limited to a single neighborhood in Antalya

items.title: Developing a climate responsive X minute city framework for walkability planning in Bahrain
items.headline: A new walkability framework for hot-arid cities
bullets: Created a climate-responsive minute city framework for Bahrain's hot-arid context.
Found that traditional proximity models fail without thermal comfort integration.
Informs planning by combining accessibility, shade, cooling, and transit.

plain.question: How can cities with very hot weather plan for people to walk easily?
plain.method: Reviewed literature, compared policies, and used computer mapping for Salman City.
plain.finding: Standard walking models do not work in extreme heat without adding cooling and shade.
plain.why: Helps design better neighborhoods where people can safely walk to everyday services.

full.explainer: Cities in the Gulf region are small enough for close-by planning, but their extreme heat makes walking very difficult. This paper looks at Bahrain, a hot place where people mostly use cars. Because standard proximity models do not work well in hot-arid environments, the authors created a new concept called the Climate-Responsive X-Minute City framework. This idea updates normal access planning by including thermal comfort and whether the climate allows people to walk outside. The researchers used a literature review, policy study, and a geographic information system test for Salman City. They mapped walking access to services and transit within different time limits. The new framework includes six dimensions: neighborhood access, land-use variety, walking infrastructure, public transport, climate adaptation, and governance. Testing it in Salman City helped find service gaps and showed how to prioritize future changes. Overall, this study helps connect shade, greening, and cooling with neighborhood planning in hot cities.
caveats: The GIS analysis is only an illustrative diagnostic for Salman City.
Not stated whether long-term health or actual behavioral changes were measured.
